# Concepts

Three ways to tell Rafael's story, each built from a different form of his own trade. All three answer some version of the line he gave us himself: "I make dashboards people actually use."

---

## Concept A — The memo

**The question.** What has to be true before someone trusts a number enough to act on it?

**The form** — the analysis memo, the first thing he named as what he works from:
1. Question *(opening — his name, the question who's asking)*
2. Data *(where from — the places and years, as evidence)*
3. What I did *(how — his way of working)*
4. What I found *(what, and what came of it — the work shown working, then the outcomes, Beatriz's words folded in as evidence)*
5. What I would do *(the close — his answer, and how to reach him)*

**The object** — a deck of eight index cards, recognisable at rest as a small stacked deck. Each carries one real thing on its face: a job, a number, the hackathon team, the Beatriz quote, Lisbon Rent Map's visitor count.

**What it becomes.**
- *Question:* the deck opens from a single card bearing the question, written as if just typed.
- *Data:* cards spread and line up left to right into a timeline — Porto, Porto, Lisbon, by year.
- *What I found:* cards turn face-up as exhibits — one becomes a line from 5 hours to 2, one becomes Beatriz's sentence, one becomes the rent map's 3,000.
- *Close:* cards square back into a single stacked deck, the top card now his contact details.

**What it stands on:** every confirmed job, number, and quote in the fact sheet.

**What it needs from him:** nothing further to build; a real screenshot later would only replace a card, not change the shape.

**Why it's his:** the memo's five-part shape is the exact ritual he said he works from — not a layout borrowed for the occasion.

---

## Concept B — The dashboard

**The question.** What makes a dashboard something people actually open?

**The form** — a dashboard's own anatomy, the second thing he named:
1. Title bar *(opening — his name, the question, loading in)*
2. Date range *(where from — jobs and years as a time filter)*
3. Filters *(how — his tools: SQL, dbt, Tableau, Power BI, as filter chips)*
4. Charts *(what — the work shown working: the Helix hours line, the rent map, AutoPilot's weekly run)*
5. KPI tiles *(what came of it — 200+ staff, 3,000 visitors, 60% faster, 6 users, a team of 5)*
6. Annotation *(what others say — Beatriz's line, as a note pinned to the chart it's about)*
7. Export *(the close — one tile left, his contact details, like a share link)*

**The object** — nine rectangular tiles, sitting at rest as a dashboard grid, grey and empty until the story gives them something to show.

**What it becomes.**
- *Title bar:* tiles sit as loading skeletons, then resolve into his name as the question types in above them.
- *Charts:* tiles expand into the real shapes — one draws the 5-to-2-hour line, one outlines Lisbon by parish, one ticks off six users running AutoPilot.
- *KPI tiles:* tiles flip to oversized numbers, one per confirmed figure.
- *Export:* the grid collapses into a single tile — his name, role, and how to reach him — the dashboard, closed.

**What it stands on:** the same confirmed facts as A, arranged by what a dashboard actually contains rather than what a memo contains.

**What it needs from him:** nothing further; it's built entirely from numbers already confirmed.

**Why it's his:** a dashboard isn't a decoration here — it's the actual thing he builds for a living, so the object and the subject are the same thing.

---

## Concept C — The weekly report

**The question.** What turns a week of work into something someone else can act on by Monday?

**The form** — the weekly report, the third thing he named, and the one AutoPilot exists to fill in:
1. Period *(opening — "Week of…", his name, the question as the header)*
2. This week's work *(where from / what — jobs and projects, one per sheet, shown working)*
3. Headline numbers *(what came of it — the same confirmed figures, framed as this week's results)*
4. Flagged *(what others say — Beatriz's line, styled as a flagged item, good news instead of a risk)*
5. Next steps *(the close — his answer, and how to reach him)*

**The object** — a desk pad of eight tear-off sheets, sitting at rest as a stacked pad with one week showing on top.

**What it becomes.**
- *Period:* the top sheet of the pad carries the question as its header, dated.
- *This week's work:* sheets peel off one at a time and lay out left to right — Atlantico, DataTugas, Helix, Meridian, Lisbon Rent Map — a timeline made of torn-off weeks.
- *Headline numbers:* each sheet's small print enlarges into the real figure it was hiding — 2 hours, 3,000, 6, 5.
- *Next steps:* the sheets restack into the pad, the visible sheet now showing his contact details.

**What it stands on:** the same confirmed facts, read through the rhythm of a recurring report rather than a one-off document.

**What it needs from him:** nothing further to build.

**Why it's his:** the weekly report isn't borrowed — AutoPilot, one of his own real projects, exists specifically to fill one in every week. The object is the exact artefact his work produces on a schedule.

---

## Which I'd choose

**Concept B, the dashboard.** Rafael's own line — "I make dashboards people actually use" — already names the dashboard as the thing that connects every job and project he has. Making the object a dashboard means the medium and the message are the same thing on screen, which gives the thirty-second read ("oh, this person builds dashboards, and this page is one") without a word of explanation. It's also the most visually alive of the three for a scroll-driven 3D build: tiles loading, expanding into real charts, and flipping to numbers gives the "things move as you scroll" feeling asked for, built entirely from data he's confirmed rather than invented screens.

A and C are both honest and workable — C in particular has a nice detail (AutoPilot literally produces the form the object is built from) — but B is the tightest fit to how he described himself and to what the site needs to do for him: get a product analyst job by proving, in the page itself, that he can make a dashboard someone wants to open.

# Storyboard — Rafael Costa, "The Dashboard"

Concept B, decided. The question the page answers: **"What makes a dashboard something people actually open?"**

The object: eight tiles, the real shape of a dashboard panel. At rest they sit as a loose grid, grey and unlit, like a dashboard that hasn't loaded yet. One tile per real, confirmed thing: Atlantico Telecom, DataTugas, Helix Genomics, FraudShield, Lisbon Rent Map, the Health Data Hackathon, Meridian Bank, AutoPilot. At the close, all eight become one.

## The chapters

| # | Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title bar | Title bar | Opening | His name, role, the tagline, and the question | 8 grey, unlit tiles sit in a loose grid; one resolves early | Nav rail to any chapter; a "skip to contact" link |
| 2 | Date range | Date range | Where from | The places and years, 2018 to now | Tiles leave the grid and line up left to right by start date | Hover/tap a tile for its name and dates |
| 3 | Filters | Filters | How | His toolkit: SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI, dbt, Statistics | The row holds; six filter chips appear beside it | Hover a chip for a one-line note on how he uses it (not tied to one tile — see Decided for you, item 5) |
| 4 | Charts | Charts | What | Each tile's real shape, drawn from its own numbers | Tiles leave the row and expand into a loose wall, each its own chart | Tap a tile for a short panel: what it was, his part, what came of it |
| 5 | KPI tiles | KPI tiles | What came of it | The headline numbers, enlarged | The wall tightens into a grid; each tile flips to a number | Same tap, same panel |
| 6 | Annotation | Annotation | What others say | Beatriz Lima's line | The grid holds; only the Helix tile gains a pinned note | Tap the pin for the line in full, with her name and title |
| 7 | Export | Export | The close | The question, answered; how to reach him | All eight tiles travel inward and merge into one | Download CV, email link, back to top |

## The beats

### 1. Title bar — Opening

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | 1 | 8 tiles, grey, in a loose unlit grid — a dashboard not yet loaded | Nothing — a quiet loading shimmer | His name and role typing in above the grid | "Rafael Costa — Product Analyst. I make dashboards people actually use." |
| 1.2 | same screen, continued | Same grid; the Meridian tile alone resolves | "200+" with a small "staff" label | The question types in beneath his name | "What makes a dashboard something people actually open?" |

### 2. Date range — Where from

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | 2, scroll drives the move | Tiles leave the grid and travel into one row, left to right by start date | Each tile shows only a name and a year: DataTugas '18, Atlantico '20, Helix '21, FraudShield '22, Lisbon Rent Map '23, Hackathon '23, Meridian '24, AutoPilot '24 | A thin ruler beneath the row, marking the years | "Porto, then Lisbon. Eight things built since 2018." |

### 3. Filters — How

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | 1 | The row holds | Tiles unchanged | Six chips appear below the row: SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI, dbt, Statistics | "The same six tools, on every one of these." |

### 4. Charts — What

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | 3, one cluster of tiles per screen | Tiles leave the row one at a time and expand into a loose wall | Helix → a line falling from 5h to 2h. Lisbon Rent Map → an outline of Lisbon's parishes. AutoPilot → six ticks, one per weekly run. FraudShield → a still notebook page over a scatter of transaction dots. DataTugas → twelve dots gathered into one cluster. Hackathon → a small bar chart. Atlantico → a narrowing funnel. Meridian → a field of small counted figures | Nothing beyond the tiles | Per tile, on tap — see panel text below |

**Panel text, written from the fact sheet, shown when a tile is tapped:**
- **Helix:** "The dashboard that tracked samples through the sequencing core, and the weekly scheduling report. The report went from about five hours to about two — my own work, not the lab's. I never touched the science."
- **Lisbon Rent Map:** "A map of what a room costs, parish by parish, across Lisbon. Mine alone. About 3,000 visitors a month."
- **AutoPilot:** "A script that fills in my team's weekly report from SQL. Six people use it."
- **FraudShield:** "My MSc capstone — a notebook working on a public dataset of card transactions. Never real-time, never run anywhere live."
- **DataTugas:** "A study group of twelve of us at university. I started it."
- **Hackathon:** "Health Data Hackathon, 2023. A team of five — I made the charts."
- **Atlantico Telecom:** "An internship. Churn analysis."
- **Meridian Bank:** "Dashboards used by 200+ staff. [Nothing further can be shown — under a confidentiality agreement.]"

### 5. KPI tiles — What came of it

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | 1 | The wall tightens back into a grid; each tile flips once | Oversized numerals: 200+, 60%, 3,000, 6, 12, 5 | A small unit label under each: staff, faster, visitors/month, users, people, teammates | "None of these are the lab's, or the team's alone, except where it says so." |

### 6. Annotation — What others say

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | 1 | The grid holds still; only the Helix tile gains a pinned note | "Rafael's dashboards changed how the core plans its week. He is the reason we stopped double-booking the sequencers." — Beatriz Lima, Head of the Sequencing Core, Helix Genomics Institute | A small pin/flag shape on the Helix tile | *(the quote is the caption)* |

### 7. Export — The close

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1 | 2 | All eight tiles travel inward and merge into one | His name, role, email, a CV link, the tagline once more | The question reappears, answered | "A dashboard people actually open is one that answers a question they already had. — Get in touch." |

## Someone with thirty seconds

The first screen (beat 1.1–1.2) carries his name, his role and tagline, and one proof — the Meridian tile resolving to "200+ staff" before any scrolling is needed. A nav rail down the side jumps straight to any chapter. A single "get in touch" link in the rail skips straight to the close, with his email and CV, without reading anything in between.

## Without the scene

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | The 8 tiles stack into a single column instead of a grid or row. The date-range travel becomes a vertical list, ordered the same way. Tap replaces hover throughout. Chapters change by a straight cut between settled states rather than a camera move, to keep it light. The filter chips wrap onto their own line. |
| With reduced motion | No camera movement and no in-between animation. Each chapter simply shows its own settled state (grid, row, wall, grid-of-numbers, pinned note, merged tile) as the visitor scrolls past it, with a plain fade. Nothing is removed — only the motion between states. |
| With no WebGL | The 3D canvas doesn't render. Each chapter instead shows the same beat as a flat, static layout — styled boxes in CSS/SVG, same numbers, same text, same tap-to-expand panels. No fact or figure is lost, only the sense of a physical object. |
| With no JavaScript | A single plain HTML page, all chapters in document order, all captions and panel text present as ordinary text (not hidden behind taps). Tiles render as static cards. The nav rail becomes plain anchor links. The CV is a direct download link; contact is a plain `mailto:` link. |

## The look and the type

Three looks, named from the object's own material — a dashboard panel:

1. **Night shift** — ground: near-black graphite. Ink: off-white. Accent: a single warm amber, the colour of a dashboard's "live" indicator. Tile surface: dark glass, a faint grid-line texture, like a BI tool in dark mode.
2. **Morning standup** — ground: warm off-white. Ink: near-black. Accent: a cobalt blue. Tile surface: light card, soft shadow, thin hairline borders — a clean light-mode dashboard.
3. **Printout** — ground: pale graph-paper grey-blue. Ink: dark navy. Accent: a red pen-mark red, for flags and annotations. Tile surface: paper-white with a faint dot grid — closer to a printed weekly report than a screen.

He picks by scrolling through all three once the site is built.

Two typefaces: a humanist sans for all running text and captions, and a monospace with tabular figures — the kind a dashboard actually sets its numbers in — for everything printed on a tile's face (the years, the KPIs, the tool names).

## Everything else the site needs

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page (nav rail + skip-to-contact) | Build | Rafael, by picking Concept B, which needs it for the thirty-second read |
| A page for each project | Never — a tap-to-expand panel on each tile instead, not a separate page | Decided for him — see `decided-for-you.md` |
| Every project listed | Build — all 8 confirmed items get a tile; none held back | Decided for him — he has few enough that nothing needs padding or cutting |
| How to reach him, and a CV | Build — but his email on the resume (`rafael@example.com`) and the project link (`rentmap.example`) both read as placeholders. **Need from him:** his real email, and a CV file to link | Open — his to give |
| What others say | Build — the Beatriz Lima quote, pinned to the Helix tile | Rafael confirmed it's usable |
| Languages | English only, for now | Decided for him — every source he gave is in English. **To confirm:** does the Lisbon job market change this? |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | Build later — a one-line description plus a still frame of the tile grid for the link preview, and a small tile shape as the favicon | Decided for him, wording to be checked with him nearer build |
| The page for an address that is not there (404) | Build — in his voice: a single tile reading "no data for this view" | Decided for him |
| A blog | Never, for now — nothing in the material calls for one | Decided for him |
| A chat | Never — adds no proof the fact sheet supports | Decided for him |
| A legal notice | Later, and only if the site adds analytics or a contact form that stores data — neither is planned yet. **To confirm:** does he want visitor analytics at all? | Open — his to decide |

## What you ask for

A yes to this script, or what to change.

What was decided for you along the way is in `docs/story/decided-for-you.md` — in short: no invented screenshots (the object is built from your real numbers instead), `rentmap.example` stays unlinked until you give the real address, "what you learned from" was left out, and no page exists for each project — each tile expands in place instead.

Two things still need you directly before anything is built: a real email address (and a CV file) for the close, and whether you want the real Lisbon Rent Map URL linked.

## On a phone, and without the 3D

- **Phone:** tiles stack into one column instead of a grid or row; the timeline becomes a vertical list; tap replaces hover; chapters cut rather than fly between states.
- **Reduced motion:** no camera movement — each chapter just fades into its settled state.
- **No WebGL:** the same beats render as flat, static CSS/SVG layouts — same numbers, same text, same tap panels, just no 3D object.
- **No JavaScript:** one plain HTML page, everything in document order, CV as a direct download, contact as a plain `mailto:` link.
